Date: 2020-12-18
REMARKS
Claims 21-50 were previously pending. Claims 21 and 23-25 have been amended. Claim 22 has been cancelled without prejudice to, or disclaimer of, the underlying subject matter. Claims 1-20 were previously cancelled without prejudice to, or disclaimer of, the underlying subject matter. Support for the claim amendments may be found in the original claims and specification; e.g., at [0009] of the as-filed specification. No new matter enters by way of the present amendment. Entry of the amendment and reconsideration of the application based on the following remarks is respectfully requested.
I. After Final Consideration Pilot
Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner consider this Response After Final based on the After Final Consideration Pilot (AFCP) 2.0. A Certification and Request for Consideration under the After Final Consideration Pilot Program 2.0 (Form PTO/SB/434) is being filed concurrently herewith.
II. Advisory Action
Applicant filed an Amendment and Response to Final Office Action ("Response") on September 23, 2020. In an Advisory Action issued on October 23, 2020, the Examiner did not enter the proposed amendments as they allegedly "raise new issues that would require further consideration and/or search," and they allegedly "are not deemed to place the application in better form for appeal." Advisory Action at 2. The arguments previously presented in the Response are reproduced in the following Sections III-V for the convenience of the Examiner.
Applicant thanks the Examiner for his consideration of the Response, and his detailed explanation in the Advisory Action. Applicant previously argued that there is no motivation to combine the cited references U.S. Publication 2002/0143262 ("Bardy"), U.S. Publication 2016/0278692 ("Larson"), U.S. Publication 2017/0007153 ("Tonar"), and U.S. Publication 2011/0191122 ("Kharraz Tavakol").
A. Motivation to Combine
In the Advisory Action, the Examiner alleges that he "used two motivations." Advisory Action at 3. In particular, the Examiner alleges that he "satisfies the finding of the invention of Bardy contain a method which differs from the claimed invention (the citation of paragraph [0008] meets this)." Id. The Examiner further alleges that the treatment of pressure ulcers is taught in [0012] of Larson and that "one can replace the limitation taught by Larson into the limitation of Bardy to obtain predictable results." Id. The Examiner points out that [0008] of Bardy states that "the invention can be capable of diagnosing symptoms of other diseases, not just myocardial ischemia," and he directly relates the teaching of "symptoms of other disease" to pressure ulcers. Finally, the Examiner brings in Tonar for teaching SEM values, stating that it "falls in line with the combination of Bardy and Larson references because they, in combination, teach a method related to pressure ulcers. The Tonar reference is related to pressure ulcers." Id. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Although obviousness can be established by combining or modifying the teachings of the prior art, "[t]he mere fact that references can be combined or modified does not render the resultant combination obvious unless the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art." M.P.E.P at § 2143.01(III) (emphasis in original). That is, just because any two references can be combined does not mean it will be combined by one of ordinary skill in the art. Here, the claimed subject matter involves (i) a method of using (ii) a measurement modality to care for (iii) a condition. The Examiner has cited (i) Bardy and Kharraz Tavakol for the method, (ii) Tonar for the measurement modality, and (iii) Larson for the condition. The primary reference, Bardy, is directed to an automated system and method for diagnosing and monitoring myocardial ischemia and outcomes thereof. Bardy provides that its systems and methods may be used for "other diseases and health disorders with similar or related etiological indicators and for those other disorders that may have an impact on myocardial ischemia." Bardy at [0095] (emphasis added). Accordingly, Bardy as a whole, taken alone or in combination with the other references, at best provides systems and methods where the use is limited to diseases with similar etiologies or related to myocardial ischemia. The Examiner has not shown how pressure ulcers are similar etiologies or related to myocardial ischemia. Instead, the Examiner has limited his reading of Bardy to [0008], focusing only on the words "other diseases," to justify his substitution of "other diseases" for pressure ulcers as taught in Larson. Applicant asserts that one of ordinary skill in the art would not have combined Bardy, Larson, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol.
B. Cited references do not teach each and every element of claims "The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious. . . . [R]ejections on obviousness cannot be sustained with mere conclusory statements." M.P.E.P. § 2142, 9th Ed. (March 2014) (internal citation and inner quotation omitted). It is well-established law for an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 103 that the references, either alone or combined, must provide all of the elements of the claim. The Office is required to make "a searching comparison of the claimed invention - including all its limitations - with the teaching of the prior art." In re Ochiai, 71 F.3d 1565, 1572 (Fed. Cir. 1995), and CFMT v. Yieldup Intern. Corp., 349 F.3d 1333, 1342 (Fed. Cir. 2003). When "[t]he prior art reference (or references when combined) [do] not teach or suggest all the claim limitations, . . . Office personnel must explain why the difference(s) between the prior art and the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art." M.P.E.P. at § 2141 (III). Here, no prima facie case of obviousness can be established at least because the cited references, either alone or in combination, do not provide all of the elements of the claims, nor do they teach or suggest the modifications that would be required to achieve the claimed subject matter.
Regarding Claim 1, the Examiner alleges that Kharraz Tavakol provides "identifying a current intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting." Office Action at 14. Applicant respectfully disagrees. Without acquiescing to the rejection, and solely to advance prosecution, Applicant has amended Claim 1 to recite "identifying a current PU intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting, wherein the current PU intervention of level-K is provided in a transfer record." Kharraz Tavakol at best provides methods and apparatus for managing physician referral processes, whereby a referring physician refers a patient to another physician for a particular medical procedure, analysis, or care. Kharraz Tavakol at [0001]. Kharraz Tavakol does not provide or suggest identifying a current intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting, wherein the current PU intervention of level-K is provided in a transfer record, as required by amended Claim 1. Thus, Bardy, Larson, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol, taken in combination, do not teach each and every element of amended Claim 1.
For at least these reasons, Applicant submits that noprimafacie case of obviousness can be established. Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner reconsider and withdraw the rejection of claim 1 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 based on Bardy, Larson, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol. "[I]f an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious." In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Thus, dependent claims 23-50, should also be allowable due to their dependence from Claim 21.
C. Improper Use of Hindsight
The Examiner alleges that he "used both KSR rationales and TSM rationales to address the combination of references. These rationales are supported within the MPEP and do not result in impermissible hindsight (see MPEP 2143)." Advisory Action at 3. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
As discussed above, a person of ordinary skill in the art would have lacked the motivation to combine at least Bardy with Larson and Tonar. Furthermore, the Examiner has not shown how one of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to combine Bardy, Larson, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol. The Examiner purportedly cites Kharraz Tavakol for providing "identifying a current intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting," a characterization to which Applicant respectfully disagrees with for the reasons discussed above in section B. Office Action at 14. Rather, Kharraz Tavakol at best provides methods and apparatus for managing physician referral processes, whereby a referring physician refers a patient to another physician for a particular medical procedure, analysis, or care, and is silent on any interventions, much less a current intervention. Kharraz Tavakol at [0001]. As Kharraz Tavakol does not provide or suggest identifying a current intervention of level-K, any understanding that it does, must have been reconstructed from the Examiner's understanding of the Applicant's disclosure. Since any motivation to combine the Kharraz Tavakol with the rest of the cited references can only be in view of the Applicant's disclosure, Applicant submits that the Examiner appears to be using impermissible hindsight to improperly interpret the claimed subject matter as obvious over Bardy in view of Larson in view of Tonar and in further view of Kharraz Tavakol.
III. Claim Objections'
The Applicant thanks the Examiner for the indication that the claim objections have been overcome by Applicant's amendments to the claims in the Amendment filed April 21, 2020.
IV. Rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 112
The Applicant thanks the Examiner for their careful consideration and indication that the rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 112 have been overcome by Applicant's amendments to the claims in the Amendment filed April 21, 2020.
V. Rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 103
A. Claims 21-25 and 28
The Examiner rejects claims 21-25 and 28 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 for allegedly being unpatentable over U.S. Publication 2002/0143262 to Bardy ("Bardy"), in view of U.S.
2016/0278692 to Larson et al. ("Larson"), in view of U.S. Publication 2017/0007153 to Tonar et al. ("Tonar"), and further in view of U.S. Publication 2011/0191122 to Tavakol et al. ("Kharraz Tavakol"). See id. at p. 11. The Examiner acknowledged that "the substitution rational[e]" is used to combine the references. Id. at p. 3; see also p. 14.
Specifically, regarding claim 21, the Examiner alleges that Bardy provides 1 Applicant filed an Amendment and Response to Final Office Action ("Response") on September 23, 2020. In an Advisory Action issued on October 23, 2020, the Examiner did not enter the proposed amendments as they allegedly "raise new issues that would require further consideration and/or search," and they allegedly "are not deemed to place the application in better form for appeal." Advisory Action at 2. The arguments previously presented in the Response are reproduced in the following Sections III-V for the convenience of the Examiner.
a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient having or at risk of developing pressure ulcers (PU) during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting, the method comprising the steps of: . . . making a plurality of measurements at a body location on the patient at the second care setting, . . . determining whether the value exceeds a threshold, . . . continuing to administer the current intervention if the value does not exceed the threshold, .
. . administering a new intervention of level-N if the value exceeds the threshold, where N has a value greater than K (emphasis omitted).
Id. at pp. 11-12. The Examiner also acknowledges that Bardy "does not explicitly teach SEM measurements, calculating a delta value, and determining if that delta value exceeds a threshold." Id. at p. 13.
The Examiner then cites to Larson alleging that Larson provides for "PU intervention as an intervention" and further alleges that "[o]ne of ordinary skill in the art could have substituted the detecting of pressure ulcer disease for the diagnosing of diseases in Brady." Id.
The Examiner further cites Tonar for allegedly providing SEM measurements, calculating a delta value by a difference between two of the plurality of SEM measurements. See id. at pp. 13 to 14. The Examiner continues to alleges that it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to substitute the SEM values provided by Tonar "for myocardial ischemia measurements and myocardial ischemia threshold values as disclosed by Bardy and Larson et al. in combination since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of the elements." Id. at p. 14.
The Examiner also acknowledges that Bardy fails to specifically provide "identifying a current intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting (emphasis omitted)." Id. at p. 13. The Examiner then cites Kharraz Tavakol and alleges that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have found it obvious to identify a current intervention of "level-K received by the patient at the first care setting as taught by Kharraz Tavakol in the method as taught by Bardy, Larson et al., and Tonar et al. in combination with the motivation(s) of preventing delays in medical care and preventing patient dissuasion from treatment protocol compliance." Id. at p. 15. Applicant respectfully disagrees with the Examiner. The Applicant submits that the Examiner has not established aprimafacie case of obviousness for at least the following reasons.
1. No motivation to combine
The burden for establishing aprimafacie case of obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) falls entirely upon the Examiner. See In re Piasecki, 745 F.2d 1468, 1471-72 (Fed. Cir. 1984). To establish aprimafacie case of obviousness, there must be some teaching, suggestion, or motivation, either in the references themselves or in the knowledge generally available to one of skill in the art, to modify the reference or to combine reference teachings. See Manual of Patent Examining Procedure ("M.P.E.P") at § 2143. There must also be a reasonable expectation of success. See id. The teaching or suggestion to make the claimed combination and the reasonable expectation of success must both be found in the prior art, and not based on the applicant's disclosure. In re Vaeck, 947 F.2d 488, 20 USPQ.2d 1438 (Fed. Cir. 1991). Although obviousness can be established by combining or modifying the teachings of the prior art, "[t]he mere fact that references can be combined or modified does not render the resultant combination obvious unless the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art." M.P.E.P at § 2143.01(III) (emphasis in original). Furthermore, "[t]he proposed modification cannot render the prior art unsatisfactory for it intended purpose." M.P.E.P at § 2143.01(V). Lastly, to reject a claim based on the substitution rational, the Examiner has the burden to establish
(1) a finding that the prior art contained a device (method, product, etc.) which differed from the claimed device by the substitution of some components (step, element, etc.) with other components;
(2) a finding that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art;
(3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have substituted one known element for another, and the results of the substitution would have been predictable; and
(4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness M.P.E.P at § 2143 B.
The Examiner alleges that "[o]ne of ordinary skill in the art could have substituted the detecting of pressure ulcer disease [in Larson] for the diagnosing of disease in Bardy." Office Action at p. 13. The Applicant respectfully disagrees. Here, the Examiner has not met the basic criteria to establish aprimafacie case of obviousness, and has not demonstrated that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have found suggestion or motivation in the references themselves, or in the knowledge generally available to a person of ordinary skill in the art, to modify the reference or to combine the reference teachings. Further, the Examiner has not met the simple substitution criteria and set out in the M.P.E.P at § 2143 B.
A person of ordinary skill in the art, when reading the disclosures of Bardy would not simply substitute the detection of pressure ulcer disease as allegedly found in Larson for the diagnosis of "other diseases" as described in Bardy due to the lack of any level of predictability.
See Bardy at [0095]. Specifically, a person of ordinary skill in the art, when reading Bardy as a whole, would be directed to a "system and method for providing diagnosis and monitoring of myocardial ischemia for use in automated patient care throughout disease onset, progression, regression, and status quo." Bardy at [0002]. Further, a person of ordinary skill in the art would be directed to Bardy seeks to detect "trends in regularly collected physiological and chemical data indicative of the onset, progression, regression, or status quo of myocardial ischemia diagnosed and monitored using an automated remote patient care system." Id. at [0008]. In fact, Bardy provides that "[o]ther benefits include an automated, expert system approach to the cross- referral, consideration, and potential finding or elimination of other diseases and health disorders with similar or related etiological indicators and for those other disorders that may have an impact on myocardial ischemia." Id (emphasis added). Here, the Examiner has not pointed to how myocardial ischemia is at all related to pressure ulcers let alone how a person of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to combined the disclosures of Bardy with Larson with predictability.
Further, the Examiner alleges that it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art to substitute SEM measurements as provided by Tonar "for myocardial ischemia measurements and myocardial ischemia threshold as disclosed by Bardy and Larson et al. in combination since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of the elements." Office Action at p. 14. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
The Examiner has not articulated all the elements for the simple substitution rationale as outline in the M.P.E.P at § 2143 B.
As described above, a person of ordinary skill in the art would not have been motivated to combined the teachings of Bardy and Larson. Further, and as described in Applicant's response dated April 21, 2020, Bardy and Tonar are directed to two different pathologies. Therefore the proposed modification of Bardy by Tonar renders Bardy unsatisfactory for its intended purpose. Specifically, and as demonstrated above, Bardy provides for the elimination of other diseases and health disorders with similar or related etiological indicators that may have an impact on myocardial ischemia. See Bardy at [0095]. The Examiner has not, at a minimum, shown that pressure ulcer has similar or related etiological indicators that may have an impact on myocardial ischemia. Accordingly, a person of ordinary skill in the art reading Bardy would not have substituted SEM values used for detecting pressure ulcers for measurements of myocardial ischemia with any level of predictability. As such, the Examiner's proposed modification renders Bardy unsatisfactory for its intended purpose, there is no suggestion or motivation to make the proposed modification, and the Examiner has not met the basic criteria to establish a prima facie case of obviousness.
2. Improper use of hindsight
The M.P.E.P warns against relying on impermissible hindsight when carrying out the obviousness analysis. Specifically, the M.P.E.P states "to reach a proper determination under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner must step backward in time and into the shoes worn by the hypothetical 'person of ordinary skill in the art' when the invention was unknown and just before it was made ... ." Further, "[k]nowledge of applicant's disclosure must be put aside in reaching this determination . .. Ilmpermissible hindsight must be avoided and the legal conclusion must be reached on the basis of the facts gleaned from the prior art." M.P.E.P § 2142 (emphasis added).
Here, it appears that the Examiner has applied impermissible hindsight to improperly interpret the claimed subject matter. As discussed above, a person of ordinary skill in the art would have lacked the motivation to combine at least Bardy with Larson and Tonar. Since any motivation to combine the cited references can only be in view of the Applicant's disclosure, Applicant submits that the Examiner appears to be using impermissible hindsight to improperly interpret the claimed subject matter as obvious over Bardy in view of Larson in view of Tonar and in further view of Kharraz Tavakol.
For at least the reasons cited above, the claims are not obvious over Bardy in view of Larson in view of Tonar and in further view of Kharraz Tavakol. Applicant understands the rejection to claim 21 under 35 U.S.C § 103 should be overcome in view of the above. "[I]f an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious." In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Thus, dependent claims 22 to 25 and 28 should also be allowable due to their dependence from amended claim 21. The Applicant reserves the right to submit further arguments shall the Examiner find claim 21 obvious.
Applicant respectfully requests the Examiner reconsider and withdraw the obviousness rejection of claims 21 to 25 and 28.
B. Claims 26, 29, 30, 37, and 38
The Examiner rejects claims 26, 29, 30, 37, and 38, under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Larson, in view of Tonar, further in view of Kharraz Tavakol as applied to claim 21, and further in view of U.S. Patent 6,738,798 to Ploetz et al. ("Ploetz").
See Office Action at p. 18. The Applicant respectfully disagrees.
"[I]f an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious." In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Without establishing claim 21 is obvious over Bardy in view of Larson, in view of Tonar, and further in view of Kharraz Tavakol, the Examiner has not established claims 26, 29, 30, 37, and 38 are obvious over Bardy in view of Larson, in view of Tonar, further in view of Kharraz Tavakol, and further in view of Ploetz. The Applicant reserves the right to submit further arguments shall the Examiner find claim 21 obvious. Applicant respectfully requests the Examiner reconsider and withdraw the obviousness rejection of claims 26, 29, 30, 37, and 38.

"[I]f an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious." In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). The Examiner rejects claims 35 and 36 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Larson, in view of Tonar, further in view of Kharraz Tavakol, further in view of Ploetz, further in view Heaton as applied to claim 32, and further in view of, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 8,355,925 to Rothman et al. The Examiner rejects claim 45 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy, in view of Larson, in view of Tonar, further in view of Kharraz Tavakol as applied to claim 21, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 8,011,041 to Hann ("Hann").
